subject: geography

moments.title: Kyoto Protocol adopted
moments.body: 11 December 1997: the Kyoto Protocol is adopted. Annex I (developed) countries commit to binding emissions reductions averaging around 5% below 1990 levels by 2008-2012. The protocol introduces emissions trading, the Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation as flexibility tools.
moments.takeaway: Kyoto was the first international climate treaty with binding targets — but only for developed countries. Developing countries (including China and India) had no targets.

moments.title: US withdrawal and entry into force
moments.who: George W. Bush administration and remaining signatories
moments.body: March 2001: the Bush administration rejects ratification, citing economic costs and the absence of binding developing-country commitments. Kyoto enters force 16 February 2005 after Russia's ratification meets the threshold (countries accounting for 55% of Annex I 1990 emissions).
moments.takeaway: The largest emitter (US at the time) was outside the binding framework. China overtook the US as the largest annual emitter around 2006.

now.title: Kyoto's legacy
now.body: The Doha Amendment (2012) extended Kyoto's targets to 2020. The EU largely met its first-period commitments. Annex I emissions overall fell, partly through outsourcing manufacturing to non-Annex countries. The Paris Agreement (2015) replaced Kyoto's top-down binding-targets model with bottom-up national pledges (NDCs).
now.open_questions: Was Kyoto effective? Defenders point to declining EU emissions and the institutional precedent. Critics point to global emissions rising and the US opt-out.

reflection: Climate diplomacy has cycled between binding (Kyoto) and pledged (Paris) approaches. Kyoto's lesson is that binding targets do not bind countries that won't accept them — and that any framework excluding major emitters is structurally limited.
